ai-3d8bd39005.headline: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
ai-3d8bd39005.fulltext:
OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI.
The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September.
However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported.
Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment.
OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn.
News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%.
The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July.
Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not.
Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI.
Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks.
Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race.
Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month.
OpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance at a valuation of $852bn.
Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn, valuing the company at $965bn.
On Friday, it emerged that Masayoshi Son, the founder of Japanese investment company SoftBank, is seeking to raise up to $100bn from Gulf states as he scales up his already mammoth investments in AI.
SoftBank has aggressively pivoted towards AI, including making a $65bn investment in OpenAI, and discussions have been held with Gulf investors including the United Arab Emirates, the Financial Times reported.
Last month, SoftBank raised $11.1bn in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally on record, paying investors yields as high as 9.75%, to fund its bets on AI and semiconductor assets.

ai-85d27ed9f5.headline: India AI Regulation Paper Due Next Month, Says Vaishnaw
ai-85d27ed9f5.fulltext:
India will release a consultation paper on AI regulation next month, focusing on data safety and homegrown technology.
Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said on Thursday that the government has decided how AI will be regulated going forward.
The paper will cover safety, cybersecurity, the benefits and harms of AI, and how to make sure every section of society gains from it.
It will also look at deepfakes (fake videos or audio made with AI), cyber threats and algorithmic harm, meaning unfair results from automated decisions.
MeitY Secretary S Krishnan warned on Thursday that privately owned AI models carry a risk.
Indian data could travel abroad, and those models could learn from whatever Indian users feed them.
Krishnan said India needs a judicious mix of approaches to protect its strategic autonomy, which means keeping control over its own technology choices.
Sources reports that the country is turning towards open-source and open-weight models, which can run inside India without sending data out.
Officials also want to build the full AI chain at home, from computing hardware to data, models and apps.
India has deployed more than 38,000 GPUs so far. These are the processors that train and run AI models.
IndiaAI Mission CEO Abhishek Singh told the sources in February that the country should have roughly 100,000 by the end of 2026.
Most of these chips still come from abroad through approved compute providers. That leaves India open to supply disruptions and high import costs.
The government approved Semicon 2.0 in July 2026 with an outlay of Rs 1,27,500 crore.
It aims to support Indian chip design, fabrication units and advanced packaging.
A PIB release puts approved manufacturing projects at 12 under the first tranche of the programme, with Rs 1.64 lakh crore committed.
The IndiaAI Mission began in March 2024 with a budget of Rs 10,371.92 crore over five years.
The paper has not been released yet, so the exact rules are still unknown. Details should become clear once it is published next month.

global-economics-f6e4801a24.headline: Zetwerk eyes ₹27,000 crore IPO valuation as over 30 investors weigh anchor book
global-economics-f6e4801a24.fulltext:
Zetwerk, a business-to-business (B2B) manufacturing platform, is preparing to tap the public markets as it seeks to capitalise on growing investor interest in India's industrial growth story.
The company is looking to launch its initial public offering (IPO) in the next few weeks at a valuation of around ₹27,000 crore ($3.1 billion), according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The IPO is expected to comprise a fresh issue of ₹2,830 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of ₹2,200 crore by existing investors.
Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Norway's central bank, and the asset management arms of Goldman Sachs, SBI and HDFC are among more than 30 foreign and domestic investors considering participation in Zetwerk's anchor book ahead of its IPO, said the first of the two persons cited earlier, both speaking on condition of anonymity.
"There is a diversified book that includes mutual funds and key FIIs. The company is likely to be valued at around ₹27,000 crore," said the second person, adding that more investors would be added to the anchor book by Sunday night.
The company said it would announce the price band of the IPO on Monday, 12 October.
Other marquee investors that have expressed interest in the anchor book include SBI Pension Fund, BlackRock, Edelweiss Asset Management and Norges Bank, Norway's central bank.
The company is expected to file its red herring prospectus (RHP) with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) within the next two weeks. the people said.
Norges Bank and SBI Pension Fund said they had no comments, while Abu Dhabi Investment Authority declined to comment. Zetwerk did not immediately respond to Mint’s email seeking comment. Mint also reached out to SBI Mutual Fund, HDFC AMC, Edelweiss AMC, Goldman Sachs AMC, and BlackRock for comment but did not receive a responses by press time.
Founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan, Vishal Chaudhary, Ankit Fatehpuria and Rahul Sharma, Zetwerk runs on its proprietary software platform, Zetwerk OS, which manages sourcing, production planning, supplier coordination and project execution. The company operates through its own facilities and a network of third-party manufacturers, supplying products to a wide range of sectors, including utilities, renewable energy, consumer electronics, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, space and defence, oil and gas, industrial automation and aerospace, both in India and overseas.
Zetwerk recorded an estimated operating revenue of ₹15,900 crore in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), up 24% from fiscal year 2025 (FY25), Inc42 reported in June, citing a rating rationale from Crisil Ratings.
Zetwerk is preparing to enter the public markets at a time when investor sentiment remains subdued, particularly towards technology stocks. The Nifty IT index has fallen 24% so far in 2026, significantly underperforming the benchmark Nifty 50, which has declined 14%. The weak market sentiment could make investor demand and pricing key determinants of the success of Zetwerk's IPO, market participants said.
In an October report, Axis Direct said that “the IT Services is likely to report relatively moderate earnings growth (in Q2FY27), as global demand remains cautious.”
However, ramp-ups in large deals, outcome-based engagements and rising AI-led spending should lend some support. Margins are expected to remain mixed, with wage hikes, AI investments, deal ramp-up costs and acquisitions weighing on profitability, partly offset by rupee depreciation and productivity gains, the brokerage added.
Since its founding, Zetwerk has raised a total of $931 million across 20 funding rounds as of 27 September, according to Tracxn data, with the last round raised early this year valuing it at $4 billion. Zetwerk is backed by investors including Greenoaks Capital, Khosla Ventures, Accel, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Peak XV Partners, Avenir Growth Capital, and Baillie Gifford.
The Bengaluru-based company has appointed Kotak Mahindra Capital, JM Financial, Avendus Capital, Pantomath Capital, and the Indian arms of HSBC, Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs as merchant bankers for its IPO.
Recent technology listings have seen mixed fortunes. ArMee Infotech, which listed on 30 September, opened flat but ended its debut session 21% lower. Fractal Analytics listed at a nearly 3% discount to its issue price on 16 February and closed the day down about 6%. In contrast, ESDS Software Solution made a strong debut on 4 September, listing at a premium of more than 76% and ending its first trading day up 109%.
Zetwerk's clients span a range of industries, from industrial heavyweights such as L&T, NTPC and Indian Oil to consumer electronics brand boAt and global companies such as Siemens, Acer and Schneider Electric. Other clients include National Aluminium Company Ltd (Nalco), CG Power Solutions, Nordex, Bharat Bijlee and Mortenson.

world-4a93d4d6cc.headline: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
world-4a93d4d6cc.fulltext:
US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
- Published
The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.
However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.
They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims.
The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel.
The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.
It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.
But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.
Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.
He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution.
The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function.
Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty".
The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".
It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment."
This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself.
The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law.
Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines.
The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes.
He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines".
"[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence.
Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others.
However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals.
  - Published18 August

indian-startups-950fbd6567.headline: Indian AI Startup Funding Surges 265% YoY In Q3, Will Momentum Continue?
indian-startups-950fbd6567.fulltext: AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in the July-September quarter, with startups in the segment raising their highest-ever-recorded quarterly funding. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding surged 265% year-on-year to $438 Mn. The number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025. The momentum builds on a strong first half of the year. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, more than four times the $162 Mn raised in the corresponding period last year. With another $438 Mn raised in Q3, the sector’s funding for the first nine months of 2026 stood at $1.1 Bn+. The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, even as the deal count fell 13%. Quarterly funding also remained below the $3.4 Bn raised in Q3 2024 and the eight-quarter average of about $2.7 Bn. AI was not the only segment to record a significant increase in investor interest during Q3. Cleantech startups raised $433 Mn, up 267% YoY, while funding for advanced hardware and technology startups, including robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% to $290 Mn. Meanwhile, fintech funding fell 11% YoY to $249 Mn, while ecommerce funding declined 31% to $245 Mn. The divergence suggests that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. But with valuations under scrutiny and large funding rounds driving the headline numbers, the question is whether AI can sustain its momentum in the coming quarters. Investors Want More Than AI Exposure Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that about 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half of the investors who see valuation froth expect a correction within the next 18 months. Another 31% see mild froth but believe valuations are supported by real revenue. Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said the rise in AI valuations is part of a global trend, particularly in the US. At the pre-seed stage, he said, valuations are often shaped more by capital requirements, future potential and acceptable founder dilution than by revenue or profitability multiples. For instance, a startup raising $3 Mn at 20% dilution would imply a $15 Mn post-money valuation, assuming the investor agrees to that price. Beyond valuations, investors are also becoming more selective about the AI applications they expect to create the most value. Vertical AI applications across sectors such as BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting this segment to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. Indian-language and sovereign foundation models received 14% of investor votes. Data, tooling and evaluation, and AI infrastructure and compute received 3% each. Obhrai said foundation models and AI infrastructure typically have longer gestation periods than venture investors prefer. Vertical AI, by contrast, offers a clearer path towards building a defensible business through distribution. “Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said. An investor who requested anonymity made a similar distinction, pointing to the capital required to scale foundation models and model-routing infrastructure. Such businesses may have to operate at nil or negative gross margins for extended periods, a commitment that Indian venture capital firms find difficult to sustain given their smaller asset bases compared with their US counterparts. The investor added that application-layer businesses could offer more durable revenue opportunities than model-routing or foundation-model companies. While some investors are backing small language models and task-specific model developers, the capital required to build and scale the underlying technology remains a constraint. The findings suggest that rising AI funding is not translating into an indiscriminate appetite for the sector. Investors are increasingly distinguishing between businesses that can use AI to solve specific problems and those that need substantial capital to develop the underlying technology. Can AI Sustain The Funding Momentum? The scale of the funding increase raises questions about how much of the momentum reflects a broad-based expansion in investor activity and how much is attributable to large growth-stage rounds. The investor who requested anonymity said funding figures need to be assessed after accounting for sizable Series B and Series C transactions, including rounds raised by companies such as Emergent. “One would have to normalise by excluding large Series B or Series C cheques,” the investor said, adding that, in their assessment, absolute AI funding had not moved significantly after accounting for these larger rounds. This distinction matters because a small number of large transactions can lift aggregate funding without necessarily signalling that more investors are deploying capital across the sector. Obhrai expects AI to retain a strong share of startup funding, even if capital flows fluctuate between quarters. However, he warned that a broader global AI bubble bursting could trigger a correction, given what he described as arguably inflated valuations of companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Several structural factors could continue to support investment in Indian AI startups. In its H1 report, Inc42 highlighted the transition of enterprise AI adoption from pilots to production, global hyperscalers’ investments in Indian AI infrastructure, and efforts to build sovereign AI infrastructure and foundation models as drivers of the sector. However, India's AI funding pool remains much smaller than the capital being deployed globally. The H1 report noted that Indian AI startup funding was still a fraction of global investment, even as companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic raised multi-billion-dollar rounds during the same period. For Indian startups, this gap presents both an opportunity and a constraint. Growing enterprise adoption and demand for specialised applications could support further investment, but businesses requiring substantial capital to develop foundational technology may find it harder to compete with better-funded global peers. The Q3 numbers establish AI as one of the biggest drivers of Indian startup funding in 2026. Whether that momentum continues will depend on more than the size of the next funding round: investors will be watching for sustainable revenue, defensible applications and valuations that can withstand a potential correction in the global AI market. indian-startups-1553a7b15a.headline: AI Startup Manus Raises $500 Million After China Nixed Meta’s $2 Billion Acquisition
indian-startups-1553a7b15a.fulltext:
In brief
- Manus parent Butterfly Effect raised more than $500 million, led by Boyu Capital and IDG Capital with Tencent, HSG and ZhenFund participating, in its first round since Meta's acquisition collapsed.
- Meta announced a roughly $2 billion purchase in December 2025; China's planning agency ordered it unwound on April 27, and Manus announced in August it would resume independent operations.
- Manus reported $100 million in annual recurring revenue about eight months after its March 2025 launch; no valuation was disclosed for the new round.
Manus, the AI agent startup that Meta bought for about $2 billion before China forced Meta to give it back, has raised more than $500 million in fresh funding.
Its parent company, Butterfly Effect, confirmed the round in a WeChat post, with Boyu Capital and IDG Capital leading and existing backers Tencent, HSG (the firm formerly known as Sequoia China) and ZhenFund joining.
The company did not say how it will spend the money, only that it plans to keep hiring in China and abroad. Butterfly Effect also did not disclose a valuation, but Bloomberg previously reported it was eyeing a $500 million raise at a $4 billion valuation, roughly double what Meta agreed to pay.
Manus makes AI agents, software that doesn't just answer questions like a chatbot but takes a goal and carries it out on its own, from booking trips to analyzing stocks. When it launched in March 2025, it sold as a Chinese rival to OpenAI's $200-a-month agent, open by invitation only.
Demand was frantic: invite codes were reportedly listed on a Chinese resale marketplace for as much as 10 million yuan, over $1.3 million. Under the hood, the company acknowledged it used Anthropic's Claude and fine-tuned versions of Alibaba's Qwen models alongside its own.
But still, these were times when agentic AI wasn’t really a big deal. Manus was experimenting with that use case before the AI behemoths started working on it.
Manus moved its team to Singapore around mid-2025, shutting most of its China operations and laying off dozens of employees in July.
By December it had reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue, the yearly total of its subscriptions, about eight months after launch. Meta announced that same month that it would buy Manus for roughly $2 billion.
Attention, meanwhile, drifted to OpenClaw, an open-source agent that runs on your own machine and takes orders through apps like WhatsApp and Telegram. OpenClaw collected well over 100,000 GitHub stars, which are developer bookmarks, within weeks of going viral.
OpenAI then hired OpenClaw's creator, Peter Steinberger, to lead its push into personal agents.
China's commerce ministry said in January it would assess the Manus deal, and by March co-founders Xiao Hong and Ji Yichao had been summoned to Beijing and barred from leaving the country, per Reuters. On April 27, the National Development and Reform Commission, China's top economic planning agency, ordered the deal withdrawn and said it would "prohibit foreign investment in Manus in accordance with laws and regulations."
Meta cut ties in June. In August, Manus announced it would operate independently again, deleting some user data created on or after December 29, 2025, to separate its systems from Meta's.
Meta's own coding agent, Muse Code, launched that same month into a market where it felt late to the fight against Codex and Claude Code. Manus, for its part, now sells Cue, an app that gives agents their own phone numbers and digital wallets, with payments limited to a budget the user sets.
The Manus case sits inside a wider tightening in Beijing: in May, China required some senior AI workers at private firms, including Alibaba and DeepSeek, to get approval before traveling abroad, as Chinese AI approaches levels of quality and relevance that can compete head to head against American companies.

global-economics-c9f9d9653c.headline: Can Trump Fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook?
global-economics-c9f9d9653c.fulltext:
[Text below is CNN's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
President Donald Trump is mounting a fresh offensive in his battle to oust Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, forming a committee of his own appointees to investigate allegations against her.
The committee will investigate alleged false statements Cook made in connection with mortgages on two properties and hold an in-person hearing at the White House on November 5, the White House announced on Friday.
Analysts say the formation of the committee and setting of a hearing date indicate Trump officials are addressing procedural issues addressed by a June Supreme Court ruling that initially blocked the administration from removing Cook.
Newly installed Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, who is also serving as acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, is one of the three members. So is National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, a staunch defender of Trump’s economic agenda, whom the president considered for Fed chair. The third member is Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
Cook’s attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, said they have been in touch with the White House “to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box-checking exercise.”
“Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her,” they said in a statement provided to CNN on Friday.
The formation of the committee marks the latest salvo in Trump’s ongoing attempts to reshape the Fed and comes just weeks ahead of its next monetary policy meeting, where officials will consider whether interest rate changes are merited.
“This seems tailor-made to address the Supreme Court’s biggest criticism in its last attempt: that Governor Cook didn’t have a chance to defend herself,” said Tim Mahedy, a former official at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, who is now CEO of research firm Access/Macro.
Mahedy said the outcome of this review “is clear” given the makeup of the committee. He expressed surprise that Hassett, a White House economist, would be on a committee investigating a legal matter about paperwork.
Trump has long berated the politically independent Fed because it hasn’t lowered interest rates to his liking, publicly targeting Cook and former Fed Chair Jerome Powell. But Trump has spared the current chairman, Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed to the position earlier this year after Powell’s term at the head of the central bank expired. Instead, Trump has insisted that Warsh is blocked by a “political” Board of Governors.
The central bank’s eight-member Board votes on interest rate decisions, along with regional Fed presidents. While the Fed leader often plays an influential role in shaping the discussion on policy moves, decisions are ultimately the result of the 12-person committee process.
At its September meeting, all 12 members, including Warsh, voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to contain inflation that has heated up largely due to the US war with Iran.
Trump said later that Warsh shouldn’t have greenlit a rate hike. “I don’t blame Kevin Warsh. I probably would have voted against the Board if I were him,” Trump said in an interview Time Magazine published earlier this month.
Separately, Trump reaffirmed he wants Warsh to “vote the way he wants.”
Trump vs. Cook
Trump previously sought to fire Cook over unproven allegations of mortgage fraud. Ultimately, in a 5-4 decision earlier this year, the Supreme Court ruled Trump could not immediately remove her.
“The 5-4 Supreme Court decision did not prohibit President Trump from firing a Fed Governor, it gave him a roadmap to do it,” Ed Mills, Washington policy analyst at Raymond James, told CNN in an email.
Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his majority opinion released in June that Cook was entitled to sufficient time and notice to respond to a termination and that she wasn’t given a fair opportunity to respond last year when Trump initially sought to remove her.
But that doesn’t mean Trump can’t lawfully fire her, he said. The law allows a president to remove Fed governors “for cause,” which is generally interpreted to mean negligence or malfeasance in the role.
The “ultimate question of whether the president can remove Cook for cause will depend in part on the underlying facts,” Roberts wrote. “We have not addressed the facts, as they have yet to be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards.”
Mills said Cook is “very clearly at risk of being fired, and it is unclear if the Supreme Court would block President Trump in Round 2.”
He added that two of Cook’s colleagues, Powell and Governor Michael Barr, are also on the list for “potential ‘for-cause’ firing.”
Kurt Lewis, a former special adviser to Powell who is now head of central bank policy at Piper Sandler, said this will ultimately come down to how much deference the Supreme Court gives the president on “cause” once justices think he has “followed a semblance of procedure.”
Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden in 2022 and is the first Black female Fed governor, with a term set to expire in 2038.
This story has been updated with additional content.

global-economics-3ed957df38.headline: Elon Musk calls Mukesh Ambani ‘Prime Minister Ambani’ in Starlink India row
global-economics-3ed957df38.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-3ed957df38.fulltext:
Elon Musk on Friday escalated his public spat over Starlink’s entry into India, sarcastically addressing industrialist Mukesh Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani” and accusing him of seeking to protect a monopoly, while asking if he would consider allowing the satellite internet service to compete in the country.
Musk’s latest salvo on X came just hours after Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia asserted that India does not permit monopolies in any sector, and that despite the buzz around one “particular” company, three players have received satcom licences and can start operations after individually meeting the security requirements and milestones.
Musk escalates Starlink row with Ambani jibe
The post by Musk now marks a sharp escalation in the Starlink satcom offering row, which saw the US trillionaire recently alleging that powerful business interests are seeking to block his service to preserve their dominance in the Indian market.
In a post on Thursday, Musk had asked if “Ambani is the real boss of India”.
On Friday evening, Musk upped the ante with a fresh post.
“Dear Prime Minister Ambani, Please accept my humble apologies for not realising that you are the real boss of India. Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?” he wrote.
Musk also said that there are many areas of India, as there are in all countries, with no internet access, which denies children the opportunity for education and small businesses the opportunity to sell their goods to a global market.
“Starlink would change their lives for the better,” Musk said.
Within minutes, Musk penned another post, saying, “Starlink has proven to be essential for saving lives during natural disasters throughout the world, when all other communication systems have failed,” adding, “So you would also be helping save men, women and children throughout India.”
Scindia says India does not permit monopolies
On Friday, Scindia said India doesn’t allow monopoly in any sector.
“Let me set the record straight. For us, the Department of Telecommunications, we are technology agnostic... Our job is to be able to provide the bouquet of services to every single customer. It is for the customer to choose in a free market which service he or she prefers, and within that service bouquet, which company’s service he or she prefers,” the Union minister said at a briefing at the India Mobile Congress here.
Scindia said that three entities – Musk’s Starlink, Reliance Jio’s satellite venture Jio Satcom and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb – have already secured licences, while Amazon’s Kuiper has expressed interest and will need to undergo the established procedure.
While there is a lot of conversation about one particular company, three have got satcom licences, he said.
“We are very clear on our stand. There are three parties that have got a licence; as and when the government decides the charge system on the revenue basis, that spectrum will be assigned to them, and as and when they individually fulfil the security conditions, they can start operations,” the minister said.
TRAI and the telecom department are close to a final decision on pricing regime for satcom spectrum, Scindia said.
Scindia criticises Congress over Starlink controversy
Hitting out at the Congress in the backdrop of Rahul Gandhi and Musk’s exchange on X, the minister said, “As far as the Congress is concerned... I don’t think they themselves know whether they’re going left or right.”
He said the Congress initially had a problem with “a certain person getting a licence” and pointed out that “now they have a problem, and they’ve allied with that person in terms of why he’s not getting a licence”.
“So I don’t know whether they have clarity on where they’re going, but that is the case with the Congress, which is to be expected,” Scindia said.
Government rejects allegations of blocking Starlink
The war of words came amid a spat over satcom services, with Musk alleging that Starlink is being blocked by certain oligarchs seeking to “maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people”.
As the India Mobile Congress (IMC) unfolded in the capital, the government and Musk traded barbs over satellite communications, with the Department of Telecommunications rejecting allegations that domestic business interests were blocking Starlink’s entry, prompting the tech billionaire to sarcastically ask whether “Ambani is the real boss of India”.
“Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license?” Musk said in an X post earlier.
The telecom ministry has maintained that the country’s authorisation framework for telecom and satellite services is “fair and non-discriminatory” and that any suggestion that it was being applied selectively was “baseless and misconceived”.

agritech-61af08bda8.headline: Monsoon May Be Over, But El Nino Is Not Done With India Yet
agritech-61af08bda8.fulltext:
Monsoon May Be Over, But El Nino Is Not Done With India Yet
El Nino may persist until early 2027, raising concerns about its potential impact on India’s next monsoon and hopes for a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.
This year’s El Nino, which played havoc with the southwest monsoon season and pushed several states including Telangana into serious drought-like conditions, may not be done yet.
With all forecasts, global or Indian, pointing to the El Nino peaking sometime in December, and the Pacific Ocean, where the phenomenon occurs, expected to record the highest-ever recorded temperatures, there are fears that its impact could linger on well into the first half of the next year. That these lingering effects might even have an adverse impact on next year’s monsoon.
At present, the ocean surface temperature in what is called the ‘El Nino 3.4 index zone’ in the Pacific, which in a non- El Nino year averages between 24 and 27 degrees Centigrade, has already hit the 30-degree mark. “The 3.4 index zone is a huge vast area. We are talking about something in the range of 61 lakh square kilometres. That is a lot of heat reserve in the water and this will take time to dissipate and return to its normal state. We are in uncharted territory as such temperatures were never recorded. So we do not really know how quickly or how slowly the cooling down will happen. This may have an impact on what happens in India in the first half of next year,” a weather scientist explained.
Once the El Nino peaks, which it is still yet to, it will have to stabilise at that stage and then start cooling down. It is already predicted that the El Nino will linger till February, or even later. “If it takes a couple of months to stabilise, and then a couple more months pass for the Pacific Ocean to reach its normal state, we are looking at a May-June timeline for the phenomenon to disappear. If this scenario plays out, then what it could mean for next year’s monsoon for India is up in the air,” the scientist said.
If the fears turn out to be true, then India’s hopes for a good monsoon next year will rest on a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) condition, something which saved the country in 1997 despite that being an El Nino year. “A positive IOD typically negates El Nino impact and the country can receive normal to near normal rains. A positive IOD also played a role in 2015. This year, the IOD was a no-show,” a meteorological research scientist said.
A positive IOD – the Arabian Sea getting warmer than the Bay of Bengal in the simplest of terms – was expected to form this year. “Overall, everybody was banking on the IOD but this did not happen. The normal period for a positive IOD to develop is sometime in July-August. We might see this happen next year. But that, as with what the monsoon will be like in 2027, is difficult to say at this point of time. The Pacific can cool down quickly, return to neutral conditions, and next year, there are hopes that the El Nino will give way to La Nina, which normally means a good rain year for the country,” the scientist said.

world-1f36d06a3b.headline: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world-1f36d06a3b.fulltext:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.
Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.
The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.
The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.
“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.
Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

work-careers-1b20ab07cb.headline: India slams JD Vance's H-1B remarks, defends Indian workers
work-careers-1b20ab07cb.fulltext:
New Delhi: India’s external affairs ministry condemned US vice president JD Vance’s description of H-1B workers as “foreign indentured servants”, calling the remarks unwarranted and deeply offensive. It also clarified that the US decision to suspend the permanent labour certification (PERM) programme for certain companies does not automatically affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of current visa holders and their dependents.
In a strongly worded statement less than 24 hours after Vance’s remarks, the ministry said Friday, “We have also seen some comments in this context by the US Vice President. We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem.”
Also Read: Green card woes deepen for Indian tech workers
Vance had made the remarks on Thursday, where he criticised the H-1B visa programme and the employer-sponsored green card (PERM) process.
PERM is distinct from H-1B’
The US leader accused companies of replacing American workers with foreign employees to reduce costs. Highlighting the contribution of immigrants to the US, the external affairs ministry said, “Indeed, the history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity. Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive.”
Also Read: US green card delays - What options do Indian tech workers have if PERM is suspended
The ministry said that the Indian government is aware of the US Department of Labor’s decision concerning the PERM programme for certain companies. “It should be noted that PERM is distinct from the H-1B visa programme,” the statement said. “The suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents, though there could be some impact on the permanent-residency/Green Card process of eligible employees of the affected companies.”
While PERM is a labour-certification process that allows eligible employers to sponsor foreign workers for green card or permanent residency, an H-1B visa is a temporary, nonimmigrant work visa for specialised occupations. The ministry stressed that talent mobility adds value to both economies. “While it creates opportunities for Indians, it equally helps US companies with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation, besides creating shareholder wealth in the US,” it said. “This is therefore an area of tremendous mutual benefit for the two countries, and our expectation is that all stakeholders in this process can appreciate this fact.
The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.” The US administration on Thursday suspended eight tech companies from the PERM green card programme as part of a wider crackdown on employment-based immigration. The move prevents these companies—Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini—from filing new permanent labour certification applications and halts the processing of pending applications under the programme.
Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft of replacing American workers with non-Americans, arguing that the company should prioritise hiring US citizens rather than foreign workers. “In the last year, Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers. At the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” he said.
US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced the decision at a press conference led by Vance, linking the action to ongoing criminal and federal investigations. It came aday after the US Department of Homeland Security proposed new fees for F-1 non-immigrant students seeking to participate in Optional Practical Training, a temporary employment authorisation programme. The department described the measure as an effort to protect American workers and strengthen the integrity of the immigration system.

global-economics-024883be95.fulltext:
BloombergUpdated9 Oct 2026, 09:35 PM IST
Jio Platforms Ltd. is set to price its shares at ₹1,065-1,119 in what's shaping up to be India's largest initial public offering (IPO), according to people familiar with the matter.
The company is targeting a market value of as much as ₹10.3 lakh crore, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t yet public. At the upper end of the price band, the Jio IPO would raise about ₹30,200 crore, according to Bloomberg calculations. That would keep it on track to become India’s largest-ever IPO.
The telecom and digital services arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries Ltd. plans to open public subscription on 21 October and close it two days later, the people said. The anchor book is scheduled to open on 19 October, with the shares expected to begin trading on 28 October, they said.
Deliberations are ongoing and details including the price range, valuation and timing could still change, the people said.
A Reliance Industries representative did not offer any immediate comments. On the sidelines of the India Mobile Congress in New Delhi Thursday, Chairman Akash Ambani said Jio Platforms aspires to deliver India's largest IPO.
The valuation falls short of some earlier expectations, though the offering is still poised to surpass Hyundai Motor India Ltd.'s ₹27,800-crore share sale in October 2024, the country’s biggest. That will be a major test of investor appetite for large share sales in one of the world’s busiest markets for equity fundraising.
Jio filed its draft prospectus in June for an offering of as many as 270 million new shares, equivalent to about 2.93% of its post-issue equity capital, according to Bloomberg calculations. The company was earlier poised to seek a valuation of about ₹11 lakh crore, people familiar with the matter have said. Valuations floated earlier were even higher, in the range of $130 billion to $170 billion at one point. A selloff in Indian stocks has since tempered pricing expectations for several IPOs in the country.
In June, Motilal Oswal Financial Services estimated Jio’s valuation at between $115 billion and $118 billion, while Dolat Capital valued the company at about $110 billion.
Jio has appointed 19 banks to work on the share sale, including Kotak Mahindra Capital Co., Morgan Stanley, Bank of America Corp., Axis Capital Ltd., BNP Paribas SA and Citigroup Inc.
Reliance Industries may offer investors a cheaper way to own Jio Platforms after the telecom unit lists, with analysts saying the parent company’s shares reflect a substantial discount.
Reliance’s share price implies a roughly 36% discount on its two-thirds stake in Jio, according to Nimish Maheshwari, co-founder of independent research firm Beat The Street. He sees about 25% as sustainable, in line with how the market values telecom rival Bharti Airtel Ltd.’s holdings in its listed subsidiaries.
Such discounts are common for parent companies because their shareholders only get indirect exposure to the businesses they own. Once a subsidiary lists, investors can simply buy its shares directly.

indian-startups-c43055e512.headline: Indian AI Startup Funding Surges 265% YoY In Q3, Will Momentum Continue?
indian-startups-c43055e512.fulltext: AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in the July-September quarter, with startups in the segment raising their highest-ever-recorded quarterly funding. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding surged 265% year-on-year to $438 Mn. The number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025. The momentum builds on a strong first half of the year. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, more than four times the $162 Mn raised in the corresponding period last year. With another $438 Mn raised in Q3, the sector’s funding for the first nine months of 2026 stood at $1.1 Bn+. The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, even as the deal count fell 13%. Quarterly funding also remained below the $3.4 Bn raised in Q3 2024 and the eight-quarter average of about $2.7 Bn. AI was not the only segment to record a significant increase in investor interest during Q3. Cleantech startups raised $433 Mn, up 267% YoY, while funding for advanced hardware and technology startups, including robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% to $290 Mn. Meanwhile, fintech funding fell 11% YoY to $249 Mn, while ecommerce funding declined 31% to $245 Mn. The divergence suggests that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. But with valuations under scrutiny and large funding rounds driving the headline numbers, the question is whether AI can sustain its momentum in the coming quarters. Investors Want More Than AI Exposure Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that about 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half of the investors who see valuation froth expect a correction within the next 18 months. Another 31% see mild froth but believe valuations are supported by real revenue. Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said the rise in AI valuations is part of a global trend, particularly in the US. At the pre-seed stage, he said, valuations are often shaped more by capital requirements, future potential and acceptable founder dilution than by revenue or profitability multiples. For instance, a startup raising $3 Mn at 20% dilution would imply a $15 Mn post-money valuation, assuming the investor agrees to that price. Beyond valuations, investors are also becoming more selective about the AI applications they expect to create the most value. Vertical AI applications across sectors such as BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting this segment to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. Indian-language and sovereign foundation models received 14% of investor votes. Data, tooling and evaluation, and AI infrastructure and compute received 3% each. Obhrai said foundation models and AI infrastructure typically have longer gestation periods than venture investors prefer. Vertical AI, by contrast, offers a clearer path towards building a defensible business through distribution. “Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said. An investor who requested anonymity made a similar distinction, pointing to the capital required to scale foundation models and model-routing infrastructure. Such businesses may have to operate at nil or negative gross margins for extended periods, a commitment that Indian venture capital firms find difficult to sustain given their smaller asset bases compared with their US counterparts. The investor added that application-layer businesses could offer more durable revenue opportunities than model-routing or foundation-model companies. While some investors are backing small language models and task-specific model developers, the capital required to build and scale the underlying technology remains a constraint. The findings suggest that rising AI funding is not translating into an indiscriminate appetite for the sector. Investors are increasingly distinguishing between businesses that can use AI to solve specific problems and those that need substantial capital to develop the underlying technology. Can AI Sustain The Funding Momentum? The scale of the funding increase raises questions about how much of the momentum reflects a broad-based expansion in investor activity and how much is attributable to large growth-stage rounds. The investor who requested anonymity said funding figures need to be assessed after accounting for sizable Series B and Series C transactions, including rounds raised by companies such as Emergent. “One would have to normalise by excluding large Series B or Series C cheques,” the investor said, adding that, in their assessment, absolute AI funding had not moved significantly after accounting for these larger rounds. This distinction matters because a small number of large transactions can lift aggregate funding without necessarily signalling that more investors are deploying capital across the sector. Obhrai expects AI to retain a strong share of startup funding, even if capital flows fluctuate between quarters. However, he warned that a broader global AI bubble bursting could trigger a correction, given what he described as arguably inflated valuations of companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Several structural factors could continue to support investment in Indian AI startups. In its H1 report, Inc42 highlighted the transition of enterprise AI adoption from pilots to production, global hyperscalers’ investments in Indian AI infrastructure, and efforts to build sovereign AI infrastructure and foundation models as drivers of the sector. However, India's AI funding pool remains much smaller than the capital being deployed globally. The H1 report noted that Indian AI startup funding was still a fraction of global investment, even as companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic raised multi-billion-dollar rounds during the same period. For Indian startups, this gap presents both an opportunity and a constraint. Growing enterprise adoption and demand for specialised applications could support further investment, but businesses requiring substantial capital to develop foundational technology may find it harder to compete with better-funded global peers. The Q3 numbers establish AI as one of the biggest drivers of Indian startup funding in 2026. Whether that momentum continues will depend on more than the size of the next funding round: investors will be watching for sustainable revenue, defensible applications and valuations that can withstand a potential correction in the global AI market. International markets across Asia-Pacific, Europe, the US, Latin America and the Middle East gained traction during the year as Juspay sought to strengthen its position as a global payments technology provider. Its core India payments business remained profitable in FY26.
The company also expanded its AI portfolio, including Xyne, an open-source enterprise AI platform designed to let organisations build applications and agents while retaining control over their data and model choices. Other offerings include Breeze Buddy, an AI voice platform, Breeze Universal for AI-led commerce discovery, and Juspay Genius, which uses AI to support payments operations and analytics.

india-deep-tech-1cd9006a3e.fulltext:
Universal Quantum Raises Record $100 Million Series A
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
Europe’s quantum computing start-ups are raising big money again, this time in Britain: Universal Quantum, a spinout from the University of Sussex, has just closed a $100 million (about €89 million) Series A round. According to the company, it is the largest Series A ever raised by a British quantum company, as tech.eu reports. That brings the start-up’s total funding to more than $125 million (about €111 million).
Roblox Founder Among the Investors
The round is led by the Silicon Valley investor DCVC and Firgun Ventures, a fund specializing in quantum technology. They are joined by Singapore’s state investor EDBI, the Japanese asset manager Integral GlobalTech, the Australian pension fund NGS Super and Roblox founder and chief executive Dave Baszucki, among others. Existing investors Nauta Capital and The Venture Collective are also participating again. Universal Quantum did not disclose a valuation.
“This round brings together investors who share the goal of delivering utility-scale quantum computing,” said Sebastian Weidt, the company’s co-founder and chief executive. Universal Quantum plans to use the money to grow in the United States, Japan and at its German site in Hamburg, and to bring its technology to market.
Trapped Ions Instead of Superconductors
Universal Quantum was founded in 2018 and is based in Haywards Heath in the English county of Sussex. The start-up relies on trapped ions: Charged atoms serve as qubits and are held in traps on a chip. Its in-house iQPU chip carries hundreds of these ion qubits and is made on a standard commercial 200-millimeter production line. The qubits are controlled with microwaves, whereas most trapped-ion systems use lasers for this. A proprietary interconnect called UQConnect is designed to link several chips into large systems, with the goal of millions of error-corrected qubits. Unlike superconducting quantum computers, which must be cooled to near absolute zero, the systems are meant to run at room temperature, according to the company.
Universal Quantum has already landed a major contract: In 2023, the start-up won a €67 million order from the German Aerospace Center (DLR), which it says is the largest ever awarded to a British quantum start-up. It also has a partnership with Rolls-Royce on fluid dynamics simulations for aerospace and several projects backed by the British funding agency Innovate UK.
Strong Competition in Trapped Ions
Universal Quantum is not alone with this approach. The German start-up eleQtron also controls ions with microwaves and raised €57 million in the spring. In Innsbruck, Austria, AQT builds trapped-ion quantum computers, and in the United States, Quantinuum and IonQ are among the industry leaders, with IonQ having acquired the British trapped-ion specialist Oxford Ionics in 2025. Big money is also flowing into other technologies: The Dutch start-up QuantWare, for example, recently raised $178 million (about €158 million) for superconducting quantum chips. Whether trapped ions, superconductors or neutral atoms will win the race to the first large, error-corrected quantum computer remains open.

beyond-your-beat-9ef20763b2.headline: 2026 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
beyond-your-beat-9ef20763b2.fulltext:
2026 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
Pillay has been instrumental in ensuring war crimes and genocide are prosecuted, Nobel committee says.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee has awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay.
The committee’s announcement of the 125th Nobel Peace Prize, made on Friday in Oslo, said the award would go to the South African jurist for her work to promote peace and international law.
It added that Pillay, a former United Nations high commissioner for human rights, had been instrumental in ensuring war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.
“At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” the committee said in a statement.
Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”. It is judges, he continued, “who guard the thin red line between order and chaos”.
Reacting to her Nobel win, Pillay, 85, said she would “dedicate this award to all of the survivors of international crimes”.
She made her statement in the historic courtroom in Germany’s Nuremberg where the trials prosecuting Nazi leaders after World War II were held.
“Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom … when the announcement was made, and I was informed of the award,” Pillay said.
She also drew attention to UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which she chaired. It concluded last year that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.
“The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza, naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay said on Friday. “One of the main reactions to that report is paying tribute to me for my courage. And you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth?”
‘A tribute’ to those defending international law
A South African of Indian Tamil origin, the 85-year-old Pillay was the first woman to start a law practice in what was then the province of Natal in 1967.
She was a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela, who previously won the Nobel Peace Prize, and other anti-apartheid activists and was the first woman of colour to serve on South Africa’s High Court.
She later served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court and as the UN’s rights chief.
The committee highlighted her role during her time on the Rwanda tribunal in establishing that rape and sexual violence can constitute crimes against humanity and genocide.
Her work on the UN inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory said last year that Israel’s president, prime minister and former defence minister had “incited the commission” of genocide.
“We concluded that the State of Israel is responsible for the commission of four genocidal acts in Gaza with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza,” she declared in a presentation to the UN General Assembly at the time.
Reacting to Pillay’s Nobel win, Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in a post on X on Friday, called it “the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice”.
Pillay currently sits on the International Court of Justice in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide against the Rohingya.
“Today’s prize is a tribute to all those working to uphold and defend international law, the rule of law and human rights, and secure peace, justice and human dignity,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reacted to the news of Pillay’s success.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the award was a “profound tribute to the veteran jurist’s courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice”.
International law ‘under political attack’
The prize, which is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), will be presented in Oslo on December 10 on the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.
Four other prizes were announced earlier this week for medicine, physics, chemistry and literature.
The Nobel committee received nominations for 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize. Other contenders included the International Space Station, emergency teams in Sudan, children’s advocates in Ukraine and two top international courts.
Ashok Swain, a researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden said that while the prize will not deliver any concrete change on the ground, the messaging of the award to Pillay is key in the current climate.
“International law … was never perfect, but at least some rules were there. Now, it has become a free-for-all, and everyone interprets it the way they want,” he told Al Jazeera.
United States President Donald Trump has long coveted the prize and repeatedly said he deserves it despite starting the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.
Last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, handed her medal to Trump after the US deposed Venezuelan former President Nicholas Maduro in January.
Pillay joked that she might share her prize with the US leader.
“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said in a video posted on social media by the secretary-general of Amnesty International that showed Pillay being applauded after the announcement of the award.
Hours after Pillay’s victory, US President Trump shared a post on Truth Social saying the Nobel committee “demeaned” the prize by awarding it to Pillay, as the White House imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
In Pillay’s comments on Friday, she denounced attacks on international legal institutions.
“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. “This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court.”

Ms. Pillay noted her journey as a lawyer in the High Court of South Africa, where she campaigned against apartheid-era discrimination, her work for justice in the Rwandan genocide of 1994, and her most recent work at the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem and Israel.
