[Text below is Al Jazeera's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
The 85-year-old South African judge has spent decades fighting apartheid and genocide.
South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the fifth South African to win it.
Making the announcement on Friday, the Norwegian Nobel Committee praised Pillay for her decades-long efforts to prosecute genocide and war crimes, which have been marked by “judicial rigour, personal integrity and considerable courage”.
From defending activists in apartheid-era South Africa, to more recently overseeing a United Nations inquiry which declared Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, the 85-year-old, who is also a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has specialised in international law for decades.
Here’s what we know about her life and why she has been awarded the world’s top peace prize:
Who is Pillay?
Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi Pillay, was born in the racially segregated city of Durban in South Africa’s Natal province in 1940 to parents of Tamil descent.
After earning a law degree from the University of Natal, she became the first woman in Natal province to start her own law firm. Early in her career, she helped defend numerous anti-apartheid activists in the country.
She later became the first woman of colour to sit on the High Court of South Africa. She went on to preside over the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), which prosecuted those charged with humanitarian crimes during the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Pillay was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) from 2008 to 2014. More recently she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory which determined last year that Israel is responsible for carrying out genocide in Gaza.
Currently, Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice, acting in a case in which Myanmar is accused of genocide against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.
What work is she best known for?
Pillay has spent much of her life advocating for human rights in her home South Africa and abroad. While studying, she took part in boycotts and marches against apartheid. She later joined the legal defence of some of the country’s most prominent anti-apartheid figures, such as Phyllis Naidoo and Strini Moodley.
In 1973, Pillay took on a case that helped secure basic rights, including legal access, for political prisoners on Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was jailed.
In a 2016 interview with the Diplomatic Courier, Pillay said her early human rights work was “shaped by what (she) had experienced under apartheid”.
“I used many of the challenges to my advantage, I had to learn international humanitarian law so as to defend cases of racial discrimination,” she said.
Pillay oversaw a UN commission of inquiry which concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
In a statement on the report, Pillay urged UN member states to do everything they can to establish a ceasefire in Gaza and to “ensure justice and accountability for all victims”.
What has she been awarded the Nobel Prize for?
The Nobel committee said Pillay was being honoured for her “efforts to promote peace and international law”.
It called her one of “the great defenders of international legal principles in our time”, having helped hold states and national leaders to account and bring “hope to victims of violence and conflict”.
The committee stressed the role Pillay played in the Rwandan genocide tribunal, saying her influence helped establish “that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide”.
“In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda,” said the committee.
Why is her win so significant?
The committee said honouring Pillay is especially important at a time when international law “is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack”.
That message was echoed by rights advocates and international officials.
The UN’s rights chief, Volker Turk, said her award was “a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security and prosperity”.
International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane said the award carried special significance “at a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law”.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa praised the award as a tribute to Pillay’s “courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice”.
Haakon Gjerlow, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, said it “sends a clear message that peace depends not only on political leadership, but on strong, credible international institutions and the courageous people who dedicate their lives to defending them .”
Ashok Swain, a professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University, told Al Jazeera that the selection of Pillay was a “pleasant surprise” and the “best possible choice”.
He said the Nobel committee likely took into consideration Pillay’s lifelong record fighting genocide and apartheid. He added that the award to the South African jurist could also be read as a message to United States President Donald Trump, who has long argued that he is deserving of the peace prize and whose administration has clashed with South Africa over debunked claims that white Afrikaners are facing “genocide”.
Furthermore, last year, the Trump administration issued sanctions against members of the ICC in what many critics saw as an attack on the system of international law.
The ICC had previously issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The ICC responded by describing the US sanctions as a “flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution” and the victims of war crimes around the world. It said it would continue its work “without regard to any restriction, pressure or threat”.
How has Pillay responded?
Pillay appeared to learn of the award as media reports circulated, telling a group of supporters applauding her: “I don’t know about this. So my question is: Is it true?”
She also jokingly referenced Trump, saying, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
Once the news was confirmed, Pillay said she would dedicate the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes”.
“This award strengthens my conviction that we must stand together in defence of the rule of law, in defence of independent courts and an international legal order based on principle.”
Earlier, the Nobel committee said it had struggled to get in touch with Pillay to notify her. “If you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up,” said committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes.

[Text below is Al Jazeera's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
2026 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
Pillay has been instrumental in ensuring war crimes and genocide are prosecuted, Nobel committee says.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee has awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay.
The committee’s announcement of the 125th Nobel Peace Prize, made on Friday in Oslo, said the award would go to the South African jurist for her work to promote peace and international law.
It added that Pillay, a former United Nations high commissioner for human rights, had been instrumental in ensuring war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.
“At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” the committee said in a statement.
Committee Chairman Jorgen Watne Frydnes said the system of international law was “under tremendous pressure” and its institutions were “under attack”. It is judges, he continued, “who guard the thin red line between order and chaos”.
Reacting to her Nobel win, Pillay, 85, said she would “dedicate this award to all of the survivors of international crimes”.
She made her statement in the historic courtroom in Germany’s Nuremberg where the trials prosecuting Nazi leaders after World War II were held.
“Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom … when the announcement was made, and I was informed of the award,” Pillay said.
She also drew attention to UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which she chaired. It concluded last year that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.
“The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza, naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay said on Friday. “One of the main reactions to that report is paying tribute to me for my courage. And you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth?”
‘A tribute’ to those defending international law
A South African of Indian Tamil origin, the 85-year-old Pillay was the first woman to start a law practice in what was then the province of Natal in 1967.
She was a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela, who previously won the Nobel Peace Prize, and other anti-apartheid activists and was the first woman of colour to serve on South Africa’s High Court.
She later served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court and as the UN’s rights chief.
The committee highlighted her role during her time on the Rwanda tribunal in establishing that rape and sexual violence can constitute crimes against humanity and genocide.
Her work on the UN inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory said last year that Israel’s president, prime minister and former defence minister had “incited the commission” of genocide.
“We concluded that the State of Israel is responsible for the commission of four genocidal acts in Gaza with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza,” she declared in a presentation to the UN General Assembly at the time.
Reacting to Pillay’s Nobel win, Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in a post on X on Friday, called it “the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice”.
Pillay currently sits on the International Court of Justice in the case in which Myanmar stands accused of genocide against the Rohingya.
“Today’s prize is a tribute to all those working to uphold and defend international law, the rule of law and human rights, and secure peace, justice and human dignity,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reacted to the news of Pillay’s success.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the award was a “profound tribute to the veteran jurist’s courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice”.
International law ‘under political attack’
The prize, which is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), will be presented in Oslo on December 10 on the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.
Four other prizes were announced earlier this week for medicine, physics, chemistry and literature.
The Nobel committee received nominations for 287 candidates for this year’s peace prize. Other contenders included the International Space Station, emergency teams in Sudan, children’s advocates in Ukraine and two top international courts.
Ashok Swain, a researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden said that while the prize will not deliver any concrete change on the ground, the messaging of the award to Pillay is key in the current climate.
“International law … was never perfect, but at least some rules were there. Now, it has become a free-for-all, and everyone interprets it the way they want,” he told Al Jazeera.
United States President Donald Trump has long coveted the prize and repeatedly said he deserves it despite starting the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.
Last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, handed her medal to Trump after the US deposed Venezuelan former President Nicholas Maduro in January.
Pillay joked that she might share her prize with the US leader.
“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said in a video posted on social media by the secretary-general of Amnesty International that showed Pillay being applauded after the announcement of the award.
Hours after Pillay’s victory, US President Trump shared a post on Truth Social saying the Nobel committee “demeaned” the prize by awarding it to Pillay, as the White House imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
In Pillay’s comments on Friday, she denounced attacks on international legal institutions.
“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. “This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court.”

Update, October 9, 2026:
OpenAI's annualized revenue rate stood at roughly $50 billion at the end of September, according to the Financial Times. The previously reported figure of nearly $70 billion (see below) was based on a calculation designed to make OpenAI's revenue more comparable to Anthropic's, Axios reports.
The gap comes down to how each company books partner sales, so it's an accounting question. Anthropic records the full customer payment when selling through cloud partners, then logs the cloud provider's cut as an expense. OpenAI only counts its own share as revenue for certain partner deals.
Both methods comply with US GAAP standards, according to Axios. The difference depends on each company's role in the transaction, meaning who controls the customer relationship and who's responsible for delivering the product.
A single report rattled chip stocks and spooked investors
After the Financial Times report landed, tech stocks took a hit, with chip stocks dropping several percent. The selloff shows how jittery the market has become and how tightly it tracks the two biggest US AI companies. That nervousness may also help explain why Anthropic is moving cautiously on its IPO and why OpenAI has already pushed its own public offering to next year.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently blamed the delay on safety risks, but the postponement was already in the works well before the cybersecurity incidents of recent months. Back in April, reports surfaced that OpenAI had missed its internal growth targets.
OpenAI still growing fast and hunting for fresh capital
Separately, OpenAI expects to actually hit an annualized revenue rate of at least $70 billion by the end of 2026, according to Bloomberg. OpenAI shared the figures during talks about a new funding round, Bloomberg says. The main driver is its expanding enterprise business, with overall annualized revenue growing 77 percent in the third quarter and enterprise revenue jumping 107 percent, CNBC reports.
The company is negotiating at least $30 billion in new capital at a target pre-money valuation of $1.4 trillion. In March, OpenAI raised up to $122 billion at a post-money valuation of $852 billion.
All of this feeds back into the AI bubble debate. Can revenue growth at AI companies keep pace with their massive spending commitments on compute buildouts over the long run? That will likely hinge on measurable productivity gains that companies can actually point to.

The government will release a draft consultation paper on regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) in the country within the next 30 days, Union Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said on Thursday.
The draft regulations will encompass key aspects such as safety and security in AI, push for a human-first approach, focus on skilling and reskilling, be inclusive on all counts and ensure that the harms are restricted, Vaishnaw said during his address at the launch of the World Bank"s World Development Report 2026 on the Promise of Artificial Intelligence.
"That consultation paper will form the basis for the regulations on AI. We have always maintained that AI cannot be regulated by just having a law. We have to take a techno-legal approach and bring such solutions.
"A bulk of these regulations will have to be undertaken by the industry," Vaishnaw said.
Earlier this year, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology constituted the Artificial Intelligence Governance and Economic Group (AIGEG), an inter-ministerial body tasked with coordinating AI policy across key ministries, their respective departments, and sectoral regulators.
India currently lacks a unified law on AI, and most governance of AI-led tools and services falls under the Information Technology Act of 2000 or the Information Technology Rules of 2022.
To ensure that government departments use AI safely and within defined parameters, the government will empanel a certain number of startups and companies.
Only these companies will be permitted to bid for AI projects for government departments at the central and state levels, he said.
In addition, to ensure adequate use of the graphics processing units (GPUs), the government will guarantee usage for up to five years in phases, so bidders are assured of the commercial value of the GPUs they onboard, he said.
The government has also floated a request for proposals to onboard another 10,000 GPUs. Of these, the government will onboard 3,000 directly for its own use, while the other 7,000 will be open to bidding by different companies, the Union minister said.
"In parallel, we are looking at other options, in the sense of how we can come up with solutions that are homegrown solutions for GPUs, at least for the inference bit in AI.
"That road map looks visible to us now," Vaishnaw said.

ai-848fdc0d50.headline: India to release AI regulation consultation paper in 30 days: Vaishnaw
ai-848fdc0d50.fulltext:
Union Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has said the government will release a consultation paper on AI regulation within 30 days. He outlined the plan while addressing the India launch of the World Bank Group's World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence, held in New Delhi on October 8.
The proposed framework comes as AI adoption expands across enterprises, public services, and digital platforms. While India is investing in computing infrastructure and domestic AI capabilities, concerns around deepfakes, cybersecurity, misuse, and accountability are becoming harder to ignore.
How India plans to regulate AI
Rather than relying entirely on conventional legislation, the government is pursuing a techno-legal approach that combines regulatory measures with technology-based safeguards.
The proposed consultation is expected to address AI safety, security, skilling, inclusion, and the responsibility of industry participants in managing potential risks.
As AI capabilities are advancing faster than traditional regulatory processes, making it difficult to address every emerging risk through legislation alone.
Technical safeguards can help organisations monitor AI behaviour, restrict unauthorised access, and identify harmful outputs. However, these measures require clear responsibilities and effective enforcement to work in practice.
Deepfakes are among the most immediate concerns. AI-generated voices, images, and videos are becoming increasingly convincing, raising the risks of impersonation, financial fraud, misinformation, and reputational harm.
The government's emphasis on technical safeguards could bring greater attention to content authentication, detection systems, platform responsibilities, and processes for responding to harmful AI-generated material.
However, identifying manipulated content is only part of the challenge. Regulators must also consider who should be held responsible for creating, distributing, and hosting such material.
For enterprises, the eventual framework could influence how AI applications are evaluated, deployed, and monitored. AI governance may become part of everyday technology procurement and risk management rather than a separate compliance exercise.
The consultation paper has yet to be released, and the government has not detailed the specific obligations that companies may face.
Who takes responsibility when AI goes wrong?
Accountability is likely to be one of the more difficult questions in India's AI regulatory discussions.
Unlike conventional software, advanced AI applications can generate unpredictable outputs, interact with external systems, and perform tasks with varying degrees of autonomy.
An enterprise using an AI application may depend on a foundation model developed by one company, cloud infrastructure provided by another, and software integration handled by a third.
When an AI system makes an incorrect decision or operates beyond its intended authority, determining responsibility becomes complicated.
The issue is particularly relevant as businesses experiment with agentic AI. These systems can execute workflows, interact with enterprise applications, and carry out tasks with limited human intervention. That makes controls over access, permissions, monitoring, and human oversight increasingly important.
A practical regulatory framework will need to address how responsibilities are shared among developers, technology providers, and organisations deploying AI.
The Centre is also considering a more structured approach to selecting companies for government AI projects.
Vaishnaw has outlined plans to empanel eligible companies and startups for AI-related work across central and state government departments. Under the proposed arrangement, participation in government AI projects would depend on meeting the empanelment requirements.
Such a process could bring greater consistency to public-sector AI procurement, particularly where applications involve citizen services, administrative processes, or sensitive information.
However, the eligibility criteria will matter. Requirements designed to strengthen security and reliability could also make it harder for smaller Indian AI startups to compete with established technology providers.
The government has yet to detail the selection criteria and assessment process.
India looks to expand its AI computing capacity
India's regulatory plans are taking shape alongside efforts to expand domestic AI infrastructure.
Through the Rs 10,372 crore IndiaAI Mission, the government is working to improve access to computing resources, datasets, and AI development capabilities.
Vaishnaw has also outlined plans for an additional 10,000 graphics processing units (GPUs), with 3,000 intended for government use and 7,000 proposed for allocation through competitive bidding.
The government is considering phased usage assurances extending up to five years, aimed at supporting infrastructure providers and improving predictability around demand.
Another area of focus is domestic AI inference capability. Inference is the process through which trained AI models generate responses, predictions, or other outputs.
As enterprises move from AI experimentation to operational deployment, inference is becoming increasingly important. Unlike model training, which requires substantial computing resources to develop AI systems, inference involves the continuing cost of running those systems.
For businesses, this brings challenges around latency, operating costs, reliability, and deployment at scale.
Developing domestic inference capabilities could help India strengthen its position in the AI value chain, although access to advanced hardware and the economics of large-scale deployment remain important considerations.
The infrastructure expansion also makes the regulatory discussion more relevant. As computing resources become accessible to more developers and businesses, the number of AI applications entering the market is likely to increase.
That growth will make security practices, monitoring, and accountability increasingly important.
What lies ahead for businesses
India's enterprise AI market is now moving beyond experimentation, with organisations exploring applications across software development, customer operations, cybersecurity, analytics, and business process automation.
As these systems become part of everyday operations, businesses will need to look beyond what AI can deliver and examine how reliably and safely it performs.
For CIO's and technology leaders, regulatory clarity could help establish consistent standards for evaluating AI providers, managing risks, and determining the level of human oversight required.
Yet regulation alone will not address the challenges of enterprise AI adoption.
Organisations must also deal with data quality, cybersecurity, workforce readiness, integration costs, and the ability to monitor AI applications after deployment.
Skilling will be particularly important. Employees need the ability to evaluate AI-generated outputs, recognise errors, and intervene when automated systems behave unexpectedly.
This makes workforce development and inclusion relevant to the government's wider regulatory plans. A framework focused only on technical compliance may overlook the organisational capabilities required to use AI responsibly.
The forthcoming consultation paper could provide greater clarity on how the government intends to balance these priorities.

Explainer: Watches win, pharma waits as Swiss-India trade deal turns one
In October 2025, Switzerland, as a member state of EFTA, entered into what was billed as a historic free trade deal with India. One year on, Swiss pharma still wants more intellectual property protection.
The promise of zero tariffs on Swiss watches in India within the next five years fuelled high spirits at a mid-September gathering of Indian and Swiss entrepreneurs hosted by the Geneva Chamber of Commerce (CCIG). In 2025, Switzerland exported CHF295 million ($354 million) worth of watches to India, a figure up 35% since 2023. Switzerland paid 22% import duties on these last yearExternal link.
The event co-organised with the Swiss-Indian chamber of commerce (SICC) came ahead of the one-year anniversary of the trade deal between India and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). Switzerland is India’s most important trading partner among the group that also includes Liechtenstein, Iceland and Norway.
“This is the most significant trade agreement worldwide”, said Vincent Subilia, the director of the CCIG.
TEPA came into force on October 1, 2025, after 16 years and 21 rounds of negotiations. Finalising the text was particularly arduous mainly due to disagreements between Switzerland and India over intellectual property rights. While Switzerland’s pharma industry is known for its innovative medicines, protected by strict intellectual property rights, India’s drug industry thrives on generic drugs that are marketed once those patents expire.
One of the biggest achievements for EFTA members was signing a deal with India before any other individual member states of the European Union, or the EU itself, and gaining preferential access to 1.46 billion inhabitants. The agreement covers key industries, such as machinery, watches and vaccine production, but leaves questions around pharmaceuticals unresolved.
In early October, on a trip to the Indian capital New Delhi to meet President Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Guy Parmelin, who holds the rotating Swiss presidency this year, commenting on the deal declared “everything isn’t perfect”. The visit included negotiations on migration and professional youth exchanges. A bilateral agreement to protect Swiss company dividends and further discussions on intellectual property were also on the agenda. Swiss pharma giants Roche and Novartis took part in the trip.
What’s in the free trade agreement?
According to the agreement, 94.7% of Swiss exports will benefit from a reduction in tariffs, with industries either immediately becoming duty free, or gradually over the next five, seven or ten years. Gold and precious metals, dairy products, finished generics and cars coming into India from Switzerland are excluded from the agreement and will continue to be taxed.
Exports of machinery to manufacture semiconductors, high-purity chemical intermediates that are used in pharmaceutical production, vaccines, and aircraft components have all become duty free since the entry into force of the agreement.
For industries including Swiss watches, chocolate, auto components, and dental equipment, tariffs have already been reduced twice: once on October 1, 2025, and once at the start of 2026. These tariffs will continue to be lowered gradually (depending on the category), until they reach zero.
How have Swiss companies benefitted so far?
Swiss goods with an immediate reduction of customs duties have had a head start compared to European Union competitors, because to date the bloc has no trade deal with India. But EU negotiations were finalised this year and an agreement may come into force in 2027. This will narrow the gap between European companies and Swiss ones.
According to Philippe Reich, chairman of the SICC and an India specialist at Baker McKenzie, Switzerland’s multinational corporations have already expanded but small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) will also benefit in the long run.
Swiss-Swedish automation company ABB announced a $75 million (CHF62.3 million) investment to expand its manufacturing and R&D capacity in 2026, and Swiss engineering firm Sulzer opened a new hub in the Indian city of Pune a month after TEPA’s launch. These investments form part of a financial commitment that is spelled out in the agreement. EFTA signatories have committed to promoting their private enterprises and institutional funds to invest $100 billion in India over the next 15 years. According to the SICC, investments announced since TEPA have reached $29 billion in Switzerland alone.
Global geopolitical shifts, including tensions between the United States and China, have been decisive for SMEs that rely on foreign supply chains. Many have shifted investments from China to India to diversify risks.
“These companies may not necessarily leave China, but they are shifting their investments from China to India. India has become more important,” said Reich.
Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE), the country’s official organisation for export and investment promotion, has said it has seen signs of increased interest from Swiss companies in the Indian market but definitive conclusions will come once they finalise their analysis of Switzerland’s economic footprint in India.
Beyond larger and more experienced consultancies, the agreement has also led to the flourishing of smaller offices. In May 2026, entrepreneur Ruby Greber set up India Swiss Enterprise in Geneva, to cater to companies looking into expanding in India.
“We help Swiss companies to establish their business in India and vice versa,” Greber explained. The consultancy is still in discussion with potential clients.
What about Swiss pharma?
While part of the pharma industry was covered by the initial deal, others such as generics were excluded. Intellectual property rights remain a key touchpoint.
According to S-GE, no new pharmaceutical companies have moved to India following the agreement. Following the agreement, Roche announced it would invest about CHF1.7 billion in India. This amount will support its existing operations and the expansion of its hub in Hyderabad, in the state of Telangana in southern India, by 2030. But the company says it hasn’t yet observed tangible benefits for its imported drugs.

Most of the company’s drugs, which range from oncology to antivirals, are imported into India as finished products and currently taxed at around 10%. Some drugs targeting rare diseases and cancer treatments have already become tax-free, but tariffs on most finished drugs will drop by 1% every year over a decade. Generics, insulin and antibiotics are excluded from the free-trade agreement and will continue to be taxed. The agreement will take longer to impact the price of these drugs.
Reich comments the real issue at stake for pharmaceutical companies isn’t so much tariffs but enhanced intellectual property rights protection, which is essential for greater pharma innovator investments in India.
India refused to grant pharmaceutical firms data exclusivity, meaning generic drugs are automatically approved based on the clinical trial data of the original drugs. The country also rejected broader intellectual property rights through which companies can extend patents beyond 20 years and conserve market exclusivity.

These talks continued during Parmelin’s visit and focused on patents and data protection during clinical trials. A spokesperson for Parmelin confirmed the exchanges were constructive and were due to continue.
“I’m absolutely convinced we will see pharmaceutical R&D in India but this is a work in progress. Companies will first need to feel comfortable about the regulatory environment from an intellectual property perspective to really go in a big way for it. But I think that’s a matter of time,” Reich said. He estimated a five-year timeline for pharmaceutical companies to seriously consider India as a research and production base.
